en: Abhidhānottara-tantra, Chapter 46: Maṇḍalavidhi (The Ritual of the Mandala), No.
1456; reproduced by Lokesh Chandra.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the mandala, the supreme of mandalas,
named the Arising of Heruka, a compendium of the essential [teachings].
The practitioner and the adept, being well-composed, should maintain the pledge.
If one initiates [disciples] into the mandala by distinguishing between the various commitments (samaya), success is not attained.
2 Honey that is red, mixed with camphor and red sandalwood—let this elixir of all remains be established in the midst of the Gaṇas. 3
One should hold the tips of the fingers of all the vajra-marked hands;
the knower of yoga should always lick [the substance] with the mouth formed by the ring finger and the thumb.
Having tasted it like the drinking of soma, one attains eternal accomplishment.
This is the fivefold nectar (pañcāmṛta), which brings about all accomplishments.
Likewise, the fourfold worship, the Virā,
and that which is entered into through the union of the two organs is the essence.

The preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) must be performed according to the rite of one hundred thousand recitations (*lakṣajāpa*). One should recite the mantra of Cakrin one hundred thousand times, or that of one's own tutelary deity (*svādhidaivata*) one hundred thousand times;
for others, one should give ten thousand (*ayuta*), and one should draw [the mandala] at the command of Cakrin.
I shall cause the mandala to be drawn for the sake of the happiness of divine and human states.
Having prepared the site as previously described, one should draw the mandala there in a location that is most excellent.
After performing the purification of the ground, it should be made exceedingly pure.
One should smear the ground of the mandala with cow dung from a drinker [of grain], making it level and free of thorns;
it should be mixed with cremation-ground ashes and endowed with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Having then smeared the ground, one should begin the mandala there;
one should perform the rite in a cremation ground.
[One should prepare it] with the charcoal dust from a funeral pyre combined with bricks from a cremation ground.
The preceptor, being well-composed, should draw the divine maṇḍala—
[he who is] complete with all auspicious marks, devoid of all inauspicious marks,
a knower of reality regarding correct cognitions, and a knower of the mantra of Śrī Heruka. || 11–12 ||
Free from anger, pure, skillful, a knower of yoga, and one who has reached the further shore of yoga;
with hair matted in a skull-bowl,
his body and limbs smeared with ashes, adorned only with sacred threads.
But he should have his hair tied in a single lock, be adorned with a garland of bones,
let a bone-garland hang down, and hold a *khaṭvāṅga* staff in his hand. [238] 14
Having made oneself Śrī Heruka, one should then visualize Heruka;
one should place him in the heart of the wheel.
Thus having armored oneself, one should place the enclosure according to the directions.
Having thus armored oneself, one should place the weapon in the center;
one should personally place oneself within the wheel, above which is a lattice of arrows,
having made oneself a cage for those who move through the sky.
Having thus donned his armor and become invulnerable even to the thirty gods,
and having thus well-protected himself and adorned with mudrās and mantras,
he should draw the formidable maṇḍala that bestows great supernatural powers (mahāsiddhi).
Then, with a thread made from a corpse and dyed with great blood,
one should delineate the formidable mandala, the excellent city of Heruka—
eight cubits or four cubits in size, square on all sides, and possessing four gates.
The practitioner of mantra should recite the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara* twice as many times while reflecting upon it.
Having established in its center a lotus with eight petals of universal colors, possessing filaments and a radiant pericarp, [he should visualize it] with leaves and endowed with stamens. (20–21)
Upon the pericarp, one should place the Hero, who has the form of Mahābhairava—
possessing vital energy, intensely radiant, with a loud laugh and a great roar;
he is crowned with a garland of skulls, three-eyed, and four-faced.
Wearing an elephant hide as his garment, with eyebrows joined by a vajra,
he should have a *khaṭvāṅga* in his hand and be adorned with one hundred and fifty garlands. Standing before him is the most formidable mudrā, Vajravārāhī.
Facing Mahābhairava, she has three eyes and a fierce form;
she is filled with skulls and entrails, with blood flowing from her mouth,
and she threatens all the quarters, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
The twenty-four ḍākinīs, born from the family of Vārāhī,
one should worship in the cardinal and intermediate directions as the nature of the wheel;
likewise, one should worship the heroes situated within the wheel.
If the practitioner desires supreme success for the Hero,
he should then prepare the ritual jars, free from roots,
black soil, and the like, adorned with pearls, gold, gems, coral, silver, and copper.
One should wrap the neck of the vessel, which is filled with all kinds of food and placed upon a skull-cup,
with a thread provided with the tips of sprouts;
having placed eight [offerings] at the doors, it should be well-wrapped with pairs of cloths.

The ninth is the central vase, wrapped in a pair of cloths; it should be adorned with silver or gold and beautified by a crest-jewel. One should scatter the entire mandala with ornaments of jewels and gold.

One should worship that beautiful city while scattering [offerings]; success is indeed certain, there is no doubt. Having sprinkled oneself and all directions with scented water, one should offer a hundred lamps if one desires the highest success.
One should mentally place all the ḍākinīs in the sky above;
those ḍākinīs who are in the world of earth, one should place them everywhere within the maṇḍala;
and whatever ḍākinīs are in the netherworld (pātāla), one should place them in the netherworld.
One should assign all the Mothers to the cardinal directions and the intermediate directions.
One should worship all those heroes situated within the Heruka maṇḍala with flowers, perfumes, and various kinds of excellent incense.
With banners described as yellow, white, black, and reddish-brown, with various beautiful garlands of flowers, and likewise with diverse kinds of garments;
With canopies, curtains, and most beautiful divine garments, provided with various kinds of food and drink, as well as solid foods and beverages.
The practitioner should first please the teacher with his whole being;
desiring spiritual accomplishment, he should worship the guru with great concentration according to his capacity.
Relying on the resonance of the bell [4], adorned with flowers and incense,
the practitioner should ring the bell with a beautiful sound, and likewise play the drum.
And one should cause a cry of "Hā! Hā! to be raised.
And having thus duly worshipped the mandala that fulfills all desires,
one should cover their faces with a cloth, O sons.
Having formed a handful of flowers and performing the *kamalāvarta* with the left hand,
one should utter the *hūṃ phaṭ* syllables while prostrating in a counter-clockwise direction;
thus established in the *ālīḍha* stance, one shall accomplish the previously mentioned siddhi.
Then, having cast a handful of flowers, one should contemplate the falling of the Kṣatriya weapon.

Then, having performed a circumambulation and being well-composed, the practitioner should enter that city; thereafter, taking recourse to Dakṣiṇāmūrti, he should again cast a handful of flowers upon the maṇḍala.
Upon whichever [deity] that flower falls, one should designate that as his lineage.
Then, being well-composed, the preceptor should perform the worship with mudrās;
and on the second day, he should cause the disciples to apply a tilaka mark made of blood after they have performed three oblations.
Then, having prepared the face of the disciple, he should show him the maṇḍala.
Wherever the abode of a deity may be, one should display this [mudrā] there.
Then, having prostrated correctly and having circumambulated the city together with the preceptor,
and having again performed the circumambulation starting from the left,
one should prostrate to the mandala and the guru according to the ritual rule.
Then, one should give the teacher the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) as prescribed by the Tathāgata.
Having bestowed a hundred thousand pieces of gold and various kinds of jewels,
as well as hundreds of pairs of garments, or even elephants, horses, and the kingdom itself.
He made ornaments for the hands with excellent necklaces, bracelets, and rings; he also provided golden sacred threads for his own wife, his daughter, and others as well.
...having prostrated with his whole being before the Self, he should make this declaration:
"From this day forward, I am your slave; I have surrendered myself to you."
Having thus performed this rite with complete certainty,
the practitioner should then offer it to him; [to him] the ḍākinīs, the mothers of yoga,
the yoginīs, the lāmās, and especially Khaṇḍarohā, [grant their favor].

Wandering through the entire world with these ḍākinīs, the practitioner— without a doubt— all things are subject to his command; he shall attain the perfection of yoga, moving unimpeded throughout the three worlds.
He may remain invisible or become a piercer of openings; he attains the power of moving through the sky (*khecaratva*) and elixirs for longevity (*rasāyana*) for the purpose of anointing his feet.
These things arise constantly and eternally for the practitioner by mere wish; furthermore, he assumes many different forms.
One travels through the sky, especially by means of a *ḍākinī*;
one subdues all living beings through the yoga taught but once, and the state of a yogin arises in an instant.
Even a mantra-practitioner who has not seen the maṇḍala, if he strives for the state of a yogin, [attains it].
He who grasps the sky with his fist and drinks the mirage—
he is the most excellent among yogins, the best, and the highest of all yogas;
he who desires this constantly shall [conquer] gods, asuras, and humans.
Having overcome [all obstacles], they shall proceed.
Whether in the *Tattvasaṅgara*, in the *Saṃvara*, or in the *Guhyavajrabhairava*,
this King of Maṇḍalas has never existed before, nor will he ever exist again.
Whatever has been said or left unsaid, all that resides within Śrī Heruka.
The forty-sixth chapter on the ritual of the maṇḍala in the Abhidhānottara.
